precepts.text: Neither had any man known her proves that to know means intercourse.
precepts.point: The whole city, both small and great, was given to this wickedness.
precepts.why:
The men of Sodom called for the men who came in to Lot, “that we may know them.” To know in scripture is to lie with. Rebekah “was very fair to look upon, a virgin, neither had any man known her.” A virgin is one no man has known, so to know means intercourse.

That is what the men of Sodom wanted with the men in Lot’s house, and it was not a few of them. “Both old and young, all the people from every quarter” compassed the house. The whole city, both small and great, was given to this wickedness.

precepts.text: Take a wife of the seed of thy fathers, as Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob did from the beginning, and their seed shall inherit the land.
precepts.point: Abraham made his eldest servant swear that he would not take a wife for Isaac of the daughters of the Canaanites, but go to Abraham's country and kindred. The Most High never condoned marrying into the other nations; the custom was kept from the beginning, way before Moses and Deuteronomy 7:3.
precepts.why:
Abraham made his eldest servant swear “that thou shalt not take a wife unto my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell: But thou shalt go unto my country, and to my kindred.” Tobit gives the same charge to his son: “chiefly take a wife of the seed of thy fathers, and take not a strange woman to wife, which is not of thy father’s tribe: for we are the children of the prophets, Noe, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.”

And he says how far back it goes: “our fathers from the beginning, even that they all married wives of their own kindred, and were blessed in their children, and their seed shall inherit the land.” The Most High never condoned marrying into the other nations. The custom was kept from the beginning, by Noe, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, way before Moses and Deuteronomy 7:3.

precepts.text: Make no marriages with the nations, for they will turn away thy son from following the Most High to serve other gods.
precepts.point: The forefathers arranged marriages. The building block of a strong nation is a strong family, and a strong family comes from marriage, not from young men and women left to their own accord.
precepts.why:
The Most High does not deal with marriage into the other nations among His chosen. Moses wrote it plainly: “Neither shalt thou make marriages with them; thy daughter thou shalt not give unto his son, nor his daughter shalt thou take unto thy son.” But Abraham had his servant swear the same thing long before Moses reiterated it: no wife for Isaac of the daughters of the Canaanites. These laws were in place from the beginning.

The law gives the reason: “For they will turn away thy son from following me, that they may serve other gods: so will the anger of the Lord be kindled against you, and destroy thee suddenly.” Solomon is the prime example. He loved women of the other nations, went into their gods, and had to repent and bring it back.

The forefathers arranged marriages. Abraham sent to his own kindred for Isaac’s wife. The building block of a strong nation is a strong family, and a strong family comes from marriage, not from young men and women left to their own accord.

precepts.text: Abraham made his servant swear the same charge for Isaac: no wife of the daughters of the Canaanites, but of his own kindred.
precepts.point: With the charge came the blessing of Abraham, passed now to Jacob and his seed: to be fruitful, to multiply into a multitude of people, and to inherit the land promised to Abraham.

note.label: Genesis 28: The Charge and the Vow at Bethel

precepts.why:
Isaac gives Jacob the charge his own father gave for him. Abraham made his eldest servant swear “that thou shalt not take a wife unto my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell: But thou shalt go unto my country, and to my kindred, and take a wife unto my son Isaac.”

Now Isaac says the same to Jacob: not of the daughters of Canaan, but of the daughters of Laban thy mother’s brother. The instruction was kept in the family line from the beginning, and with it passed the blessing of Abraham, to Jacob and to his seed with him.

precepts.text: Rebekah was born to Bethuel, son of Milcah, wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother; the marriages stayed within the kindred.
precepts.point: Jacob was sent to Laban, the son of Bethuel the Syrian, the brother of Rebekah. Rebekah herself was born to Bethuel, son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother; the family line was kept in place, generation after generation going back to their own kindred.

note.label: Genesis 28: The Charge and the Vow at Bethel

precepts.why:
Jacob was sent “unto Laban, son of Bethuel the Syrian, the brother of Rebekah.” Rebekah herself came out of that same house: she “was born to Bethuel, son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham’s brother.”

Nahor was Abraham’s brother; Bethuel was Nahor’s son; Rebekah was Bethuel’s daughter; and now Jacob goes to Bethuel’s son Laban for a wife. The family line was kept in place, generation after generation going back to their own kindred.

precepts.text: Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide; he had an appointed place and time of day, alone at the going down of the sun, to reflect on the works of the Most High.
precepts.point: Make meditation a daily custom, a holy habit, as our forefathers did: somewhere alone and peaceful where the mind can be clear, because you cannot meditate in the middle of activity and noise. When you meditate continually on the commandments, the Lord establishes your heart, and the evil thoughts you battle begin to flush out of your mind.

note.label: Joshua 1: The Charge to Joshua and the Formula for Success

precepts.why:
“And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide: and he lifted up his eyes, and saw, and, behold, the camels were coming.” Isaac had an appointed place and time of day, alone at the going down of the sun, to reflect on the works of the Most High.

Make meditation a daily custom, a holy habit, as our forefathers did: somewhere alone and peaceful where the mind can be clear, because you cannot meditate in the middle of activity and noise. Isaac went out to the field at the eventide; that is the pattern for meditating in the law day and night.

moments.label: Marriage Beyond Romance: From Eden to Modern Confusion

points: Isaac brought Rebekah into his mother's tent, she became his wife, and he loved her. She becomes his wife, then he loved her. Brothers three months into proving saying I love her usually have mommy issues. There is no love at first sight; what we call that is lust at first sight, and disorder follows when it is the primary mover.

Genesis 26:8: Abimelech looked out a window and saw Isaac sporting with Rebekah his wife. Intimacy is not just sex; it is being the truest form of yourself before your spouse, laughing and having a good time, and it came after they were married, not before. Some of you want that now, knee to knee at the school feeling the electricity, hormones clouding everything so you rationalize what you were warned about.

note.label: Marriage Beyond Romance: From Eden to Modern Confusion

points: Abraham made his eldest servant swear that he would not take a wife for Isaac of the daughters of the Canaanites, but go to Abraham's country and kindred. The Most High never condoned marrying into the other nations; the custom was kept from the beginning, way before Moses and Deuteronomy 7:3.
Abraham told the servant, The Lord God of heaven shall send His angel before thee. He trusted the oath would be fulfilled because the Most High goes before the errand.
The servant prayed for a sign at the well: the damsel who offers to draw for the camels also is the one appointed. Before he had done speaking, Rebekah came out.
Rebekah was very fair to look upon, a virgin, neither had any man known her: undefiled and beautiful, the kind of wife the forefathers had from the beginning.
When the sign came to pass exactly, the servant bowed his head and worshipped the Lord: I being in the way, the Lord led me to the house of my master's brethren.
Rebekah said, I will go. Her family blessed her: Be thou the mother of thousands of millions, and let thy seed possess the gate of those which hate them.
Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide; that was a custom of the forefathers, showing the Lord was dealing with them long before the law was written at Sinai.

When Rebekah saw Isaac she lighted off the camel, and she took a vail and covered herself. The four mothers covered their heads with actual material as a sign of submission; that is the custom 1 Corinthians 11 goes into.
Isaac brought Rebekah into his mother's tent, and she became his wife, and he loved her; and Isaac was comforted after his mother's death, for he received a righteous wife like unto his mother.

The Most High does not deal with marriage into the other nations among His chosen. Abraham made his servant swear not to take a wife for Isaac of the daughters of the Canaanites; these laws were in place long before Moses reiterated them.

The reason is given in the law itself: they will turn away thy son from following me, that they may serve other gods. Solomon is the prime example; he loved women of the other nations, went into their gods, and had to repent and bring it back.

The servant asked a sign, and before he had done speaking Rebekah came out: very fair, a virgin, and kind. She gave a stranger drink and drew for all his camels; that kind and easily entreated spirit is the pattern for the daughters of Israel.
